# Pull Requests and Builds You Can Trust {#sec-team}



The fast path reviewed an agent's change as a pull request and rebuilt it from a fresh clone
by hand (@sec-fast-pr). That last check is the one a reviewer most often skips, because it
takes time and a clean machine, and it is the one an agent's fluent summary cannot replace.
Continuous integration, CI, makes it automatic: on every pull request, a machine that has
never seen the project clones it, installs the tools, computes the results, runs the tests and
renders every page, and the pull request shows a green tick or a red cross. A guard that the
results no longer support turns it red, naming the sentence.

This chapter adds that to the Acme project, with the rules a team needs for agents' changes:
one change per pull request, nothing generated committed, and nothing called done until it has
been rebuilt. It then publishes the site from `main` and renders the monthly reports on a
schedule, both by the same build.

::: opener
- Write the rules a team's agents follow, and a pull request template a reviewer can use.
- Ask for a CI workflow that runs the project's own rebuild commands, with versions pinned
  from their sources.
- Read a red build: which step failed, and which sentence or test it names.
- Publish a site and render recurring reports from CI, and say what each costs on GitHub's
  plans.

Start from
: your `acme-eval` repository at the end of @sec-parameters, or
  `checkpoints/19-eval-params/`, on GitHub as in @sec-fast-pr.

You build
: team rules in `AGENTS.md`, a pull request template, and three workflows: a check on every
  pull request, publishing from `main`, and reports on the 2nd of each month.

Checkpoint
: `checkpoints/20-eval-ci/`
:::

::: payoff
A build that refuses a false sentence. Once one of the home page's guards no longer holds, the
render step stops, and its log names the sentence in the project's own words:

::: transcript

```default
ClaimError: The results no longer support this sentence: The release called best has the highest ROC AUC.
```


:::
:::

## What CI is made of {#sec-team-vocab}

*Continuous integration* is a build that runs by itself on every change. GitHub's is called
GitHub Actions, and its parts have names:

| Ask for | GitHub Actions calls it |
|---|---|
| a build, written down | a *workflow*: YAML in `.github/workflows/` |
| when it runs | `on:`, a *trigger*, such as `pull_request` |
| a clean machine | a *runner*: `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04` |
| a tick or a cross | a *status check* |
| "nothing reaches `main` unbuilt" | a *protected branch* |

: CI's parts, and what GitHub Actions calls them. {#tbl-team-vocab}

A workflow should run the commands you run, not new ones. The project's `AGENTS.md` already
lists its rebuild: compute the results, run the tests, render the site, check the pages. CI runs
the same four, so a green tick means what "it builds on my machine" was meant to mean.

## Rules for a team {#sec-team-rules}

A team's agents need rules a lone author can keep in their head. Each agent session starts
fresh, reads `AGENTS.md`, and does what it says, so the rules go there; each reviewer opens a
pull request, so the checklist goes in its template. Ask for them in two turns:

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Add a section "Team rules" to AGENTS.md for working in a team: work on a branch, never push to `main` or merge; one coherent change per pull request; never commit outputs/, reports/, _site/ or rendered files; before saying a change is done, run the four rebuild commands (evaluate, tests, render, check_site) and say which passed; never weaken a test or a `claim` guard to make a step pass; report what you could not verify. Do this on a new branch `team-rules` and commit it.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`git switch -c team-rules` · edits `AGENTS.md` · `git commit`
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create .github/pull_request_template.md: the three checks (scope, correctness, rebuild) as a checklist, saying what to look at for each in this project, and a line asking which agent made the change and what it did not verify. Commit it on `team-rules`.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `.github/pull_request_template.md` · `git commit`
:::

<!-- Dry-run 2026-11-25, both turns verbatim, in a copy of checkpoint 19-eval-params with no
remote: a Claude Code sub-agent on Sonnet 5.5 and one on Haiku 5.5. Both wrote the section on
a new branch team-rules, took the four commands from AGENTS.md, ran them under their own new
rule (all passed), and committed the template there as a second commit. -->

Read the diff as the reviewer of a rule book. Each rule should name this project's files and
commands, not general good practice: "never commit `outputs/`" is a rule an agent can check,
"keep the repository clean" is not. The rule against weakening a guard matters most. An agent
told to make a failing step pass has two routes, fixing the sentence or loosening its guard,
and only one is right.



A pull request changes one sentence of the model card, the second below. Its description says
"wording only".

> The call centre calls the top 10% of the list, so the business metric is recall
> in the top 10%: the share of all subscribers that those calls reach. For
> v3 it is 0\.420 (95%
> interval 0\.396 to 0\.442), against a base rate
> of 11\.7%.

The file's rows for that metric, `recall_top10`:

| `version` | `value` | `low`, `high` |
|---|--:|--:|
| v2 | 0.419818 | 0.396294, 0.442398 |
| v3 | 0.435703 | 0.413252, 0.459005 |


::: tryit
Review the pull request against `outputs/metrics.csv`, as its template's three checks ask;
@sec-checkpoints has the answer.

::: done
you can say which figure is wrong, whose it is, and which of the three checks found it.
:::
:::

## A build on every pull request {#sec-team-check}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create .github/workflows/check.yml: on every pull request and every push to `main`, on `ubuntu-24.04` with read-only permissions, install Quarto 1.10.20 and uv 0.11.32 with its cache on, then run the four rebuild commands from AGENTS.md in order. Pin each action to its latest release, the major tag where it has one, looking the versions up rather than remembering them, and tell me what you chose and where you checked. Commit it on a new branch `ci` from `team-rules`.
```
:::

The finished workflows pin actions/checkout@v7\, actions/deploy\-pages@v5\, actions/upload\-artifact@v7\, actions/upload\-pages\-artifact@v5\, astral\-sh/setup\-uv@v10\.3\.3 and quarto\-dev/quarto\-actions/setup@v2, the latest releases when this chapter was tested,
and Quarto 1\.10\.20. Ask for the versions to be looked up: an agent's memory of an
action's version is as old as its training, and an old major version can stop working when
GitHub retires what it runs on. Name the versions of the tools as well, since a prompt that
said only "uv" got that day's newest. It worked, but a build that installs whatever is newest
is not the same build next month.

::: {.you}
```bash
git push -u origin team-rules
gh pr create --base main --fill
gh pr merge team-rules --merge
git push -u origin ci
gh pr create --base main --fill
```
:::

Review the first pull request against its template's three checks, and merge it with a merge
commit, as above, so that the second shows only the workflow. The second runs the check, step
by step on its *Checks* tab; merge it when it is green.

What it costs: GitHub Actions' standard runners are free in public repositories\, and a free account's private repositories get 12 US dollars of compute a month (@sec-facts). A private repository's
check uses that allowance; a public one does not.

## A red build {#sec-team-red}

A check that has never failed has not been tested. Break a guard on purpose, on a branch you
will throw away.

::: think
You are about to break a guard on purpose. Before you push: which of the check's
four commands will fail, and why not the others?

The render, the third: the results still compute and the tests still pass, because neither
reads prose. The render runs the guard, and the `claim` quotes its sentence in the log. If the
tests went red instead, the change broke more than a sentence.
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
This breaks a guard on purpose, to see CI fail. On a new branch `try-red` from `ci`, change the condition of one `claim` guard in index.qmd so that it no longer holds, without changing its sentence, commit it, and tell me which sentence CI should name.
```
:::

::: {.you}
```bash
git push -u origin try-red
gh pr create --base main --fill --draft
```
:::

The check goes red at its render step, naming the sentence, as at the start of this chapter. That is what a teammate sees when a change to the data or the model makes a
typed claim untrue: not a report that quietly says the wrong thing, but a pull request that
cannot be merged with it. Close the pull request and delete the branch
(`gh pr close --delete-branch`).

To make "cannot be merged" literal, protect `main`: under the repository's *Settings*, add a
branch protection rule, or a ruleset, that requires a pull request and the *Check* job before
merging. One limit: on a free GitHub account\, protected branches and rulesets work in public repositories only; private repositories need GitHub Pro\, Team or Enterprise. On a free private repository the
check still runs and still shows red; it is the team's rule, not GitHub's, that nothing red
is merged.

::: practice
For this edition the check workflow was run on a local runner (act), green and then red; the
steps that need GitHub (pushes, pull requests, the uv cache, publishing, the schedule and
branch protection) were checked against GitHub's documentation, not run.
:::

## Publish from `main` {#sec-team-publish}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create .github/workflows/publish.yml: on every push to `main`, and on demand, run the same build, then deploy _site/ to GitHub Pages with GitHub's own Pages actions (no `gh-pages` branch), with the permissions and environment they need, given only to the job that deploys. Tell me the one repository setting I must change before it first runs.
```
:::

The setting is the Pages source: *Settings*, *Pages*, *Build and deployment*, *Source*:
**GitHub Actions**. Set the project's `site-url` to the address it gives, so that the social
cards of @sec-sites work. A page whose guard fails is never published, because publishing runs
the same build first. The permission to deploy belongs to the deploy job alone; say so in the
prompt: unprompted, an agent may give it to the whole workflow.

::: pitfall
Where it may go comes first (@sec-sites-publish): a free GitHub account publishes Pages from public repositories only; private repositories need a paid plan\, and a site only your organisation can see needs GitHub Enterprise Cloud. The
Acme evaluation is of public data and could be public; a client's evaluation could not, and
publishing it needs a host your organisation approves, or no site at all, only the PDFs.
:::

## Reports on a schedule {#sec-team-schedule}

The last workflow renders the monthly reports by itself, on a schedule, and keeps them for you
to download:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create .github/workflows/monthly.yml: on the 2nd of every month at 06:17 UTC, and on demand, run the same build, then `uv run python scripts/render_params.py --formats pdf`, keep reports/ as a downloadable artifact for 90 days, failing if it is empty, and run scripts/check_refs.py last. Explain the schedule line in a comment, including its time zone and why the minute is not 0.
```
:::

The finished schedule is the cron line "17 6 2 \* \*": minute 17, hour
6, day 2 of every month. GitHub reads it in UTC unless a `timezone:`
line beside it names one, such as `timezone: "Europe/London"`; it runs on the latest commit of
`main`, and may start late, or in the worst case not at all, when Actions is busy, which it is
at the top of each hour; hence minute 17, not 0. The PDFs appear as an artifact
at the foot of the run's page, kept 90 days. The reference check runs last
because it needs the network and can fail for reasons outside the project; placed last, it
fails the run without losing the reports. *Run workflow*, on the workflow's page under
*Actions*, runs it now, which is how to test it without waiting a month.

::: story
<!-- source: book/chapters/team.qmd lines 225-227 at 651db10 ("a first comment said 06:00
UTC was 07:00 in London in winter; it is 06:00, and 07:00 in summer. The agent caught it") -->
The schedule's first comment said that 06:00 UTC is 07:00 in London in winter. It is 06:00;
it is 07:00 in summer. The agent caught its own slip. A reviewer skimming a comment in a
YAML file might not have. Check any time arithmetic an agent writes.
:::

::: pitfall
GitHub turns scheduled workflows off in a public repository after sixty days with no activity.
A monthly report that matters needs someone who notices when it does not arrive.
:::

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/20-eval-ci/README.md
```
:::

::: tryit
Add the team rules and the template, then the three workflows, and break a guard on a branch
to see the check fail.

::: done
a pull request shows a green check, a deliberately broken guard turns one red naming its
sentence, and `ls .github/workflows` lists `check.yml`, `monthly.yml` and `publish.yml`.
:::
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- Rules for agents go in `AGENTS.md`, which every session reads; the reviewer's checklist goes
  in the pull request template, which every reviewer sees.
- CI runs the project's own rebuild commands on a clean machine for every pull request, so a
  green tick means it builds anywhere.
- Break a guard on purpose once: a check that has never failed has not been tested.
- Publishing and scheduled reports run the same build first, so nothing unchecked goes out.
- Pin actions to versions looked up at their source, and know what each step costs on your plan.
:::
